tldr: By focusing on a sparse 5-point reference (pelvis, wrists, and ankles) and decoupling explicit tracking error feedback from motion encoding, Anchor 1 achieves ultra-precise and stable whole-body manipulation without online retargeting.
hero_caption: System overview of Anchor 1. (A) Calibrated sparse references (5 points) are extracted from human motions via geometric calibration and paired with offline-retargeted robot motions for quality curation. (B) An error-decoupled architecture tokenizes motion references with an encoder while feeding tracking errors directly to the decoder. (C) During real-world deployment, it flexibly accepts commands from both teleoperation and high-level policies (VLA).
overview:
Whole-body manipulation with humanoid robots is a long-standing goal in robotics, but it presents severe challenges. Reaching deep into a low shelf requires delicate coordination; an accidental step or a small slip can knock the hands off-target and cause the entire task to fail. Controllers must balance precision (reaching target positions accurately) with sustained execution stability (avoiding slips and stumbles).

Existing learning-based whole-body controllers typically rely on online joint-space retargeting to map human motions onto the robot, or they compress human poses into latent motion tokens. However, online retargeting easily introduces joint discontinuities and control failures due to solver errors. On the other hand, motion token compression strips away the fine-grained signals needed to correct millimeter-level deviations.

To overcome these issues, the authors propose Anchor 1, a whole-body control architecture that limits its command interface to a sparse 5-point reference: the poses of the pelvis, both wrists, and both ankles. By avoiding online joint-level retargeting, Anchor 1 preserves kinematic redundancy for precise task execution. The remaining degrees of freedom are guided toward stable, physically natural postures learned from an offline-curated dataset of high-quality robot motions. Furthermore, explicit end-effector tracking error feedback is decoupled from the motion encoder and fed directly into the decoder, preventing execution errors from corrupting the latent motion token space.

Across extensive evaluations in simulation and on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid, Anchor 1 reduces tracking errors by 30% to 80% compared to existing state-of-the-art controllers, while dramatically cutting down foot slips and unintended steps. It also significantly boosts teleoperated data collection efficiency and delivers higher autonomous task success rates when paired with a learned VLA policy.
contributions: Proposed a control framework that eliminates online joint retargeting and completes stable whole-body coordination from geometrically calibrated sparse 5-point target poses.
Established an architecture that decouples explicit tracking error feedback from motion encoding, achieving high-precision tracking without corrupting latent motion representations.
Constructed a comprehensive three-track benchmark dedicated to whole-body manipulation to systematically diagnose tracking precision, sustained execution stability, and reachability.

Consistently demonstrated millimeter-level manipulation precision, highly dynamic whole-body coordination, efficient teleoperated data collection, and autonomous task execution on a physical humanoid.

sections.heading: The Challenge in Whole-Body Manipulation: Why Balancing Precision and Stability Is Hard
sections.summary: Operating humanoids in human-centric environments requires close coordination among the hands, torso, and feet, where even minor foot slips can ruin a manipulation task. The authors highlight the fundamental flaws of existing approaches—online retargeting failures and error-correction loss from token compression—and establish their research motivation.
sections.details:
For humanoid robots to be truly useful in daily environments, bipedal locomotion alone is not enough; their hands and feet must be coordinated with extreme precision. For instance, reaching into a low shelf couples end-effector positioning tightly with torso posture and balance. Similarly, carrying a flat tray without tilting it requires holding hand poses steady at the millimeter level while stepping. If the robot takes an unintended small step or slips on the floor—even without falling over—the hands veer off-target and the manipulation task fails.

Recent reinforcement learning-based whole-body controllers have made great progress by learning diverse motor skills from human motion capture data. However, applying these controllers to teleoperation or autonomous manipulation reveals two critical bottlenecks.

First is faithful command transmission. Traditional systems often use online inverse kinematics (IK) to retarget human motions into the robot's joint space in real time. When IK encounters singularities or solver discontinuities, the resulting joint commands spike unpredictably, jerking the robot or destabilizing its balance. Conversely, compressing human skeleton models directly into latent tokens distorts critical end-effector trajectories due to differences in skeletal proportions between humans and robots.

Second is precise error correction. While motion-token-conditioned controllers interface cleanly with high-level planners, compression blurs out the fine-grained correction signals needed for sub-centimeter adjustments. Mixing hand tracking errors directly into the motion token, on the other hand, entangles the intended motion with transient execution errors, making it difficult for high-level policies to predict and reuse clean tokens.

To solve these problems, Anchor 1 discards online joint retargeting. Instead, it takes a geometrically scaled sparse 5-point target reference (pelvis, wrists, and ankles) as input, allowing the learned distribution of offline-curated motions to resolve the remaining joint degrees of freedom. By cleanly separating the motion token from tracking error feedback, Anchor 1 achieves both a high-level policy interface and millimeter-level control precision.

sections.heading: Empirical Proof: Outstanding Precision, Stability, and Practical Utility Across Sim and Real
sections.summary: This section covers benchmark evaluations in simulation, physical robot experiments on a Unitree G1, ablation studies, and real-world teleoperation and autonomous task results. Anchor 1 clearly outperformed existing state-of-the-art baselines across precision, stability, data collection efficiency, and task success rates.
sections.details:
### 2.1 & 2.2 Benchmark Evaluations and Simulation Results
Anchor 1 was evaluated on three benchmark tracks (In-house, Public, and Reachability) and compared against ScaleBFM XL, SONIC v1.1, and MimicLite v1.1. On the In-house track, Anchor 1 (Global mode) achieved an 88.4% local success rate and an 88.7% global success rate, securing the lowest root translation error and limb tracking error among all methods. In asymmetric dual-arm reaching tasks while walking, where the strongest baseline (ScaleBFM) scored only 57.0%, Anchor 1 achieved an overwhelming 91.2% success rate. On the Public track (featuring dynamic actions like running and jumping) and the Reachability track (requiring sustained stationary support), Anchor 1 exhibited rock-solid stance control, averaging only 0.06 slips and 0.53 unwanted extra steps per sequence.

### 2.3 Physical Robot Tracking Performance
Real-world evaluations on a Unitree G1 humanoid utilized a Reachability subset (51 motions) and an In-house subset (72 motions). On the Reachability subset, Anchor 1 achieved global position errors of 44.58 mm for wrists and 35.70 mm for ankles. This significantly outperformed the strongest baseline (MimicLite at 53.59 mm and 50.40 mm), despite MimicLite requiring online retargeting and a longer look-ahead horizon (0.08 s vs. Anchor 1's 0.06 s). Compared to SONIC-SMPL, which also avoids retargeting, Anchor 1 slashed wrist and ankle tracking errors by approximately 73%. On the In-house subset under the strictest 10 cm tolerance threshold, Anchor 1 achieved the highest success rate, beating all baselines by 41.2 percentage points.

### 2.4 Ablation Studies
To identify what drives this performance, the authors conducted several ablations. In terms of end-effector trajectory fidelity (unit-PDV), Anchor 1's sparse representation had 80.2% less directional distortion than SONIC's SMPL input. While online retargeting approaches (IK-based GMR and point-cloud-based UMR) suffered control collapses from sudden joint discontinuities, Anchor 1 maintained smooth execution by consuming sparse poses directly.
Architectural comparisons showed that feeding explicit error feedback directly to the decoder rather than the encoder is crucial. Routing errors into the encoder dropped the global success rate, whereas decoder injection boosted it from 70.9% to 88.7%. Furthermore, during latent motion token interpolation tests, the error-decoupled architecture maintained far lower joint-angle RMSE, producing natural, uninterrupted postural transitions.

### 2.5 Teleoperation Data Collection and Autonomous Tasks
During teleoperation trials, Anchor 1 adapted seamlessly to four different operators (heights 165–188 cm, weights 50–80 kg) and four distinct motion capture systems (Xsens, CHINGMU, PN-LINK, and PICO VR) using only geometric calibration. In two challenging tasks—kicking a cardboard box into a target zone and retrieving slippers from a low shelf—data collection efficiency surged from 9 and 41 successful demos/hour with SONIC to 43 and 62 with Anchor 1 (with collection success rates of 98.0% and 97.4%).
When autonomous Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies (GR00T N1.7) were trained on this collected data, Anchor 1 yielded substantially higher task success rates. In particular, using reconstructed sparse targets from tokens ("Recon. feedback") preserved high task execution rates even when high-level policies issued motion tokens directly without external references.

sections.heading: Why Sparse Input and Decoupled Errors Work: Insights, Limitations, and Next Steps
sections.summary: This section discusses the kinematic redundancy provided by sparse references, the vital role of high-quality training distributions, current limitations such as single-robot validation and lack of force feedback, and future directions toward object-centric control.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Insights for Whole-Body Manipulation
The primary takeaway is the power of role allocation: specifying only task-critical end-effectors sparsely, while allowing an offline-curated, high-quality motion distribution to complete the remaining whole-body degrees of freedom. By defining only pelvis, wrist, and ankle poses, the robot can naturally adjust its torso to match its own morphology and balance requirements. This flexibility enables the robot to reach challenging targets while keeping its stance feet planted without slipping.
Decoupling error feedback from motion tokens also makes strong control-theoretic sense. Motion tokens stay focused purely on motion intent, while transient deviations are handled directly by the decoder. This separation provides high-level policies (like VLAs) with clean, expressive tokens, while allowing the low-level controller to apply high-gain, millimeter-level feedback corrections.

### 3.2 Limitations
The authors identify several limitations:
- All real-world experiments were conducted on a single platform (Unitree G1); cross-embodiment generalization across different link ratios and joint configurations remains unverified.
- Control targets are purely kinematic (positions and orientations), without explicit modeling of contact forces, grasp slip, or joint torque limits.
- When reconstructing sparse targets from motion tokens (Recon. branch), slight reconstruction errors persist, leaving a minor performance gap compared to feeding exact sparse references.

### 3.3 Future Directions
Promising next steps include incorporating object-relative coordinates directly into the control targets and extending the architecture to force-hybrid control for compliant contact tasks. Other valuable avenues involve refining the trajectory reconstruction head and establishing theoretical closed-loop stability guarantees for long-horizon, multi-contact manipulation.

sections.heading: Under the Hood: From Data Curation to the Anchor 1 Architecture
sections.summary: A deep dive into the dataset construction, automated screening pipeline, sparse reference extraction via geometric calibration, the error-decoupled encoder-decoder network, and the PPO-based reinforcement learning setup.
sections.details:
### 4.1 & 4.2 Dataset Construction and Quality Control
Training relied on approximately 1,081.4 hours of motion capture data (116.8M frames across 406,222 sequences after left-right mirror augmentation), blending proprietary captures with public datasets like AMASS. Proprietary data accounted for 77.3% of the total.
Data quality control (QC) was rigorous. Robot motions retargeted offline from human poses were screened using automated algorithms for prolonged floating, joint angle discontinuities, self-collisions, periodic jitter, and ground penetration. Proprietary sequences underwent additional full human inspection to discard any motion with unnatural artifacts.

### 4.5.1 Sparse Reference Extraction and Geometric Calibration
To accommodate differences in body proportions between human operators and the robot, a T-pose geometric calibration was applied. Without solving inverse kinematics, scale factors and rotation offsets were computed for each link, generating a robot-scaled human skeleton representation $H^{\prime}$. From this, the poses of 5 key links (pelvis, both wrists, and both ankles) were extracted as $H^{\prime}_{5}$. During deployment, only these 5 poses are passed to the controller, completely bypassing online IK solvers or joint-predicting neural networks.

### 4.5.2 & 4.5.3 Network Architecture and Reinforcement Learning
The controller comprises an encoder $E$, a finite scalar quantizer $Q$, a trajectory head $K$, and a control decoder $D$.
- Input: Poses from $H^{\prime}_{5}$ across four frames (0, 20, 40, and 60 ms look-ahead) in the robot's current root frame are fed into the encoder to produce a motion token $z_t$.
- Decoupled Error Feedback: Position and orientation errors $e_t$ between the current and target poses of wrists and ankles bypass the encoder and are fed directly into the control decoder $D$ alongside proprioceptive observations $o_t$.
- Trajectory Reconstruction Head: When operating purely on tokens $z_t$ from high-level policies, trajectory head $K$ reconstructs immediate sparse target poses so that feedback error $e_t$ can be computed autonomously.

Training was conducted via Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) in simulation. The reward function evaluated tracking against paired, high-quality robot reference motions $R$, augmented with auxiliary losses for sparse target reconstruction, future trajectory prediction, and cycle consistency.

### 4.5.4 Deployment Inference Modes
For real-world deployment, Anchor 1 offers two inference modes: a Global mode for tracking absolute trajectories, and a Re-locate mode for teleoperation. Re-locate mode translates the origin of the target reference window to the robot's actual base position from the previous frame, aligning teleoperator steps with the robot's heading without unnatural drift.

sections.heading: Appendix: Benchmark Architecture and Trajectory Fidelity Metrics
sections.summary: Details on the three evaluation tracks (In-house, Public, and Reachability) designed to probe whole-body coordination, along with the formulation of the unit-PDV metric used to measure directional fidelity.
sections.details:
### S1 Benchmark Tracks and Spatial Coverage
To comprehensively assess whole-body manipulation, the benchmark was split into three distinct tracks:
1. In-house Track (15,342 sequences): Systematically generated by combining upper-body tags (trunk flexion, unilateral/bilateral reaching) with lower-body tags (standing, walking, squatting, half-kneeling). This track covers over 90% of the coordination patterns required for daily tasks.
2. Public Track (2,230 sequences): Gathered from public datasets including BONES-SEED, CIRCLE, OMOMO, and AMASS to test out-of-distribution generalization on dynamic actions like running and jumping.
3. Reachability Track (3,210 references): Evaluates reaching specific 3D grid points from five base postures (standing, shallow squat, deep squat, split-stance, and half-kneeling), holding the target for 2 seconds, and returning. Stance foot slips and unintended steps during the hold phase are rigorously tracked.

### S2 Motion Fidelity Metric (unit-PDV)
To quantify how well an input representation preserves human motion intent, the authors introduced the normalized Pairwise Displacement Vector divergence (unit-PDV). By comparing normalized displacement vector directions over matching time intervals and scaling by arm length, unit-PDV rigorously measures whether fine hand trajectories and directional cues are preserved through retargeting or token compression.

takeaways: Specifying only task-critical points (5 points: pelvis, wrists, and ankles) and delegating full-body coordination to a high-quality learned motion prior dramatically improves precision and stability.
Replacing online inverse kinematics (IK) or retargeting with geometric calibration completely avoids singularities and joint discontinuities that trigger control failures.
Decoupling tracking error feedback from motion tokens and injecting it directly into the decoder enables millimeter-level control while providing a clean token interface for high-level VLA policies.
Evaluating whole-body controllers requires strict benchmarks that penalize stance foot slips and unintended steps alongside standard tracking error metrics.
limitations: Validation is limited to a single humanoid hardware platform (Unitree G1); cross-embodiment generalization across different link proportions and kinematics remains unverified.
The controller targets purely kinematic end-effector poses, without explicit contact force feedback, grasp stabilization, or external compliance modeling.
In token-only reconstruction mode (Recon.), minor target reconstruction errors cause a slight performance dip compared to feeding exact sparse references directly.
